lessons.title: Enzymes: Phytase, Xylanase, Protease
lessons.body:
Enzymes are proteins that break down feed components your birds cannot digest on their own. In Africa, most feed ingredients like maize, soybean meal, and wheat bran contain anti-nutritional factors that lock up nutrients. Adding the right enzyme unlocks them, saving you money on expensive ingredients like fishmeal and synthetic amino acids.

Phytase is the most important enzyme for African poultry. Up to 80% of phosphorus in plant seeds is bound as phytic acid, which chickens cannot absorb. Without phytase, you must add expensive dicalcium phosphate and your birds excrete most of the phosphorus, polluting the environment. Add 500 FTU of phytase per kg of feed. This releases about 0.1% available phosphorus, equivalent to 1 kg of dicalcium phosphate per 100 kg feed. It also improves calcium and zinc absorption. For layers, this means stronger eggshells and fewer broken eggs.

Xylanase breaks down arabinoxylans in wheat, barley, and maize by-products. These fibres form a gel in the gut, slowing digestion and causing wet litter. Adding 1,000-2,000 units of xylanase per kg of feed reduces gut viscosity, improves litter quality, and increases energy availability by 2-3%. In broilers, this can improve feed conversion ratio by 3-5 points. Use xylanase especially when your feed contains more than 20% wheat or wheat bran.

Protease digests proteins that survive normal digestion, especially in soybean meal and cottonseed meal. Adding 0.1-0.2% protease to broiler diets can reduce crude protein by 1% while maintaining performance. This lowers feed cost and reduces nitrogen excretion, which means drier litter and less ammonia. For layers, protease improves egg mass and reduces feed cost per egg.

Practical application: Buy enzyme products from reputable suppliers like DSM, Novozymes, or BASF. Store them cool and dry, away from sunlight. Mix enzymes into the feed just before feeding because they lose activity over time. Use a premix or spray them onto pellets after cooling. Always follow the manufacturer's dosage. Overdosing wastes money; underdosing gives no benefit. Test your feed ingredients firstâif your maize is high quality, you may need less xylanase. Work with a local feed lab to check enzyme activity if you suspect poor quality.

lessons.title: Probiotics, Prebiotics, and Synbiotics
lessons.body:
Probiotics are live beneficial bacteria that colonise the gut and fight off harmful microbes like Salmonella and E. coli. Prebiotics are non-digestible fibres that feed these good bacteria. Synbiotics combine both. In African poultry production, where heat stress and poor biosecurity are common, these additives are your cheapest insurance against disease and poor growth.

Probiotics for poultry usually contain Lactobacillus, Bacillus, Enterococcus, or yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae). They work by producing organic acids that lower gut pH, competing for attachment sites, and stimulating the immune system. For broilers, add 0.5-1 kg of probiotic per tonne of feed from day 1 to slaughter. This can improve feed conversion ratio by 5-8 points and reduce mortality by 2-3%. For layers, probiotics improve egg production by 2-4% and reduce dirty eggs. A common product is Bacillus subtilis (e.g., 1x10^9 CFU/g), dosed at 0.5 kg/tonne.

Prebiotics include mannan-oligosaccharides (MOS) from yeast cell walls, fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS), and inulin. MOS at 1-2 kg/tonne binds harmful bacteria and prevents them from attaching to the gut wall. This reduces diarrhoea and improves litter quality. In Africa, where aflatoxin risk is high, MOS also binds some mycotoxins, protecting the liver. FOS at 0.5-1 kg/tonne feeds beneficial bacteria like Bifidobacteria.

Synbiotics combine a probiotic and a prebiotic in one product. They are more effective than either alone because the prebiotic helps the probiotic survive and establish. Use synbiotics during periods of stress: after vaccination, during heat waves, or when changing feed. A typical synbiotic dose is 1 kg/tonne of feed.

Practical tips: Store probiotics in a cool, dry placeâheat kills them. Do not mix them with antibiotics, as antibiotics will kill the probiotic bacteria. If you must use antibiotics, wait 48 hours after the last antibiotic dose before giving probiotics. For small-scale farmers, you can make a simple probiotic by fermenting maize bran with water and molasses for 3 days, but commercial products are more reliable. Always check expiry dates and CFU counts on the label. In Africa, look for products registered by your national drug authority, such as NAFDAC in Nigeria or KEPHIS in Kenya.

lessons.title: Organic Acids and Essential Oils
lessons.body:
Organic acids and essential oils are natural alternatives to antibiotic growth promoters. They lower gut pH, kill harmful bacteria, and improve nutrient digestion. In Africa, where antibiotic resistance is a growing concern and some countries ban antibiotic growth promoters, these additives are essential for profitable poultry production.

Organic acids include formic, acetic, propionic, butyric, lactic, and citric acid. They are either free acids or salts (e.g., calcium formate, sodium butyrate). Free acids are stronger but corrosive; salts are safer to handle. Add 0.2-0.5% of a blend to broiler feed. This reduces Salmonella and Campylobacter in the gut, leading to cleaner carcasses and lower mortality. For layers, organic acids improve eggshell quality by improving calcium absorption. Butyric acid is especially good for gut healthâit feeds the cells lining the intestine. Use 0.1-0.2% coated butyrate in broiler diets.

Essential oils come from plants like oregano, thyme, cinnamon, clove, and garlic. They contain active compounds such as thymol, carvacrol, and cinnamaldehyde. These compounds disrupt bacterial cell membranes and have antioxidant effects. Add 100-300 mg per kg of feed. A common blend is 5% carvacrol + 3% thymol. Essential oils improve feed conversion by 3-5 points and reduce respiratory disease. In Africa, you can also use local plants: crushed garlic (0.5% of feed) has antibacterial properties, and dried oregano leaves (1% of feed) work well.

Practical application: Organic acids are corrosive to equipment, so use stainless steel or plastic mixers. Add them to the feed after pelleting because heat destroys some acids. For essential oils, mix with a carrier like silica or vegetable oil before adding to feed to ensure even distribution. Store in airtight containers away from sunlight. Do not use organic acids and essential oils together with antibioticsâthey may interact. In hot African climates, essential oils can evaporate, so use encapsulated forms. For small flocks, you can make a simple acidifier by mixing 1 litre of vinegar (acetic acid) with 10 litres of water and spraying on 100 kg of feed, but commercial blends are more consistent. Always follow dosage instructions and consult a veterinarian if birds are sick.

lessons.title: Antioxidants and Mold Inhibitors
lessons.body:
Antioxidants and mold inhibitors protect feed quality and bird health. In Africa, where high humidity and heat accelerate spoilage, these additives are not optionalâthey are necessary to prevent rancidity, mycotoxin production, and nutrient loss.

Antioxidants prevent fats and oils in feed from going rancid. Rancid feed smells bad, reduces feed intake, and destroys vitamins A, D, and E. Common antioxidants are ethoxyquin, BHA, BHT, and natural ones like vitamin E (tocopherols) and rosemary extract. Add 100-200 mg of synthetic antioxidant per kg of feed, or 200-500 mg of natural antioxidant. For feed with high oil content (e.g., 5% palm oil), use the higher dose. In Africa, where fishmeal and palm oil are common, antioxidants are critical. Without them, feed can spoil within 2 weeks in hot weather. Store antioxidants in a cool, dark place. Mix them into the oil before adding to feed for best results.

Mold inhibitors prevent mold growth and mycotoxin production. Molds grow when feed moisture is above 12% and humidity is high. Common mold inhibitors are propionic acid, calcium propionate, sodium benzoate, and potassium sorbate. Add 0.1-0.3% propionic acid or 0.2-0.5% calcium propionate to feed. For long storage (more than 1 month), use 0.3-0.5%. In Africa, where maize and groundnuts are often contaminated with aflatoxin, mold inhibitors alone are not enoughâyou also need mycotoxin binders like bentonite or yeast cell wall. Add 1-2 kg of binder per tonne of feed.

Practical application: Test feed moisture with a cheap moisture meter (available for $20-50). If moisture is above 12%, dry the feed before adding mold inhibitor. Mix mold inhibitors evenlyâuse a feed mixer, not a shovel. For small-scale farmers, you can use propionic acid at 0.2% by spraying on feed while mixing. Wear gloves and a mask because propionic acid is corrosive. Store treated feed in dry, ventilated bags on pallets, not on the floor. In West Africa, where humidity is very high, use both an antioxidant and a mold inhibitor. Check expiry datesâantioxidants lose potency after 6 months. Always buy from reputable suppliers and keep records of batch numbers.

lessons.title: Coccidiostats and Histomonostats
lessons.body:
Coccidiostats and histomonostats are medicines that prevent two major poultry diseases: coccidiosis and histomoniasis (blackhead disease). In Africa, where litter is often reused and hygiene is challenging, these additives are vital for broiler and layer health. However, their use is regulated, and you must follow withdrawal periods to avoid drug residues in meat and eggs.

Coccidiosis is caused by Eimeria parasites that damage the gut, causing bloody droppings, poor growth, and death. Coccidiostats are added to feed continuously or in shuttle programs. Common coccidiostats include ionophores (monensin, salinomycin, lasalocid) and non-ionophores (amprolium, toltrazuril, diclazuril). For broilers, add 100-125 ppm monensin or 60-70 ppm salinomycin. For layers, use 125 ppm monensin until 16 weeks of age, then stop because residues can appear in eggs. Amprolium is used at 125-250 ppm for treatment. Rotate coccidiostats every 3-6 months to prevent resistance. In Africa, where many farmers use traditional herbs, you can also use garlic or neem, but they are less effective than commercial drugs.

Histomoniasis (blackhead) affects turkeys and sometimes chickens, causing liver and caecal lesions. Histomonostats include metronidazole, nitarsone, and nifursol. However, many countries ban these drugs due to cancer risks. In the EU and USA, no histomonostats are approved. In Africa, check your national regulations. If histomoniasis is a problem, focus on biosecurity: separate turkeys from chickens, use clean litter, and avoid mixing age groups. Some farmers use oregano oil or garlic as natural alternatives, but efficacy is not proven.

Practical application: Always follow the withdrawal period. For monensin, withdraw 3 days before slaughter for broilers; for layers, do not use after 16 weeks. For amprolium, withdraw 3 days. Use a feed mill that can accurately mix these drugsâunderdosing causes disease, overdosing causes toxicity. Store coccidiostats in a dry place away from feed. If you see bloody droppings, consult a vet immediately. Do not use coccidiostats and histomonostats together without veterinary advice. In Africa, many governments require a prescription for these drugs. Keep records of all medicated feed. For organic production, use natural coccidiostats like Saccharomyces cerevisiae or probiotics, but expect lower efficacy.

lessons.title: Regulatory Status and Safe Use of Additives
lessons.body:
Feed additives are regulated to protect animal health, human health, and the environment. In Africa, regulations vary by country, but most follow the Codex Alimentarius or EU standards. As a feed formulator, you must know which additives are approved, at what levels, and what withdrawal periods apply. Using banned or overdosed additives can lead to rejected products, fines, and harm to consumers.

First, check your national feed law. In Nigeria, the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) regulates feed additives. In Kenya, the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) and the Department of Veterinary Services. In South Africa, the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act (Act 36 of 1947). In Ghana, the Food and Drugs Authority. Always buy additives that have a registration number and a label in English or French. Keep certificates of analysis for each batch.

Second, follow maximum inclusion levels. For example, the EU limits zinc oxide to 150 ppm in feed, and bans antibiotic growth promoters. Many African countries still allow some antibiotics, but the trend is toward restriction. For coccidiostats, maximum levels are set for each drug. For enzymes, there is no maximum, but follow manufacturer recommendations. For organic acids, levels up to 1% are generally safe. For essential oils, up to 300 mg/kg. For antioxidants, 150 mg/kg for synthetic ones. For mold inhibitors, 0.5% propionic acid.

Third, respect withdrawal periods. This is the time between the last medicated feed and slaughter or egg collection. For example, monensin: 3 days for broilers, not for layers. Amprolium: 3 days. Tylosin: 5 days. If you sell eggs, do not use any drug without checking if it is allowed for layers. Drug residues in eggs can cause allergies and antibiotic resistance in humans.

Fourth, keep records. Write down the additive name, batch number, date added, dose, and withdrawal date. This helps if there is a disease outbreak or a customer complaint. Store additives in a locked, dry, cool place away from children and animals. Wear protective clothing when mixing. Dispose of empty containers properlyâdo not burn or bury near water sources.

Finally, stay updated. Regulations change. Join a feed association, attend workshops, and read government gazettes. In Africa, the African Union Interafrican Bureau for Animal Resources (AU-IBAR) provides guidelines. When in doubt, consult a veterinarian or feed regulatory officer. Safe use protects your business, your birds, and your community.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feed Additives and Supplements in African Broiler and Layer Production

Feed additives are the smallest line item in a poultry feed budget, yet they routinely decide whether a batch of broilers reaches market weight on time or a layer flock holds peak production through the heat of an African dry season. For a commercial feed mill in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, or Zambia, additives are also the highest-margin product category and the most regulated. This lesson is a working reference: what each class of additive does, where it pays for itself, how to buy and store it, and what the law expects of you.

1. Enzymes: Phytase, Xylanase, Protease

Phytase is the single most bankable enzyme in African poultry feed. Maize and soybean meal â the backbone of most diets â contain 60â80% of their phosphorus as phytate, which poultry cannot digest. Adding phytase at 500â1,000 FTU/kg releases 0.08â0.12% available phosphorus and allows you to cut dicalcium phosphate and reduce the "P penalty" in manure. In a 50 kg batch of broiler finisher, replacing 8 kg of DCP with phytase plus limestone typically saves 2â4% of total feed cost, and the effect is larger when imported DCP is scarce or priced in scarce foreign currency.

Xylanase targets the arabinoxylans in wheat, maize bran, and other fibrous by-products common in African rations. It improves digestible energy by 2â4% and reduces wet litter. Protease improves protein digestibility and lets you lower crude protein by 0.5â1.0 percentage points, which cuts soybean meal cost and nitrogen excretion. For a commercial mill, the practical rule is: buy enzymes with a declared activity unit and a coating or granulation that survives pelleting at 80â90Â°C. Uncoated liquid enzymes added post-pelleting are the most reliable route in humid climates.

2. Probiotics, Prebiotics, and Synbiotics

Probiotics (direct-fed microbials) are live cultures â Bacillus subtilis, Lactobacillus spp., Enterococcus faecium, and yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) â that colonise the gut and compete with pathogens. Prebiotics are non-digestible oligosaccharides (MOS, FOS, GOS) that feed beneficial bacteria. Synbiotics combine both. In African conditions, where antibiotic growth promoters are increasingly restricted and heat stress suppresses gut integrity, these products earn their place in the first 10â14 days of brooding and during any disease challenge. Expect 2â5% improvement in feed conversion and reduced mortality in challenged flocks; the return is highest when the alternative is a therapeutic antibiotic.

3. Organic Acids and Essential Oils

Formic, propionic, lactic, citric, and butyric acid salts lower gastric pH, inhibit Salmonella and E. coli, and improve protein digestion. In humid storage, organic acids also act as mould inhibitors in finished feed. Essential oils â oregano, thyme, cinnamon, clove, and garlic â have antimicrobial and antioxidant activity and are popular as natural growth promoters. Blends are more effective than single oils because bacteria do not easily develop resistance to a multi-component product. Dose rates are typically 0.5â2 kg/tonne for acidifiers and 100â300 g/tonne for encapsulated essential oils.

4. Antioxidants and Mould Inhibitors

Tropical heat and humidity accelerate oxidative rancidity in fats and destroy vitamins A, D, and E. Antioxidants â ethoxyquin, BHA, BHT, and natural tocopherols â are added at 100â200 g/tonne to protect both the feed and the bird's immune status. Mould inhibitors â propionic acid, calcium propionate, and sodium benzoate â are essential when maize moisture exceeds 13% or when feed is stored for more than three weeks. Aflatoxin binders (hydrated sodium calcium aluminosilicate, yeast cell wall products) should be used whenever maize is sourced from areas with known aflatoxin risk; they are not a substitute for rejecting contaminated grain.

5. Coccidiostats and Histomonostats

Coccidiosis remains one of the top three disease costs in African broiler production. Ionophores (monensin, salinomycin, lasalocid) and chemical coccidiostats (amprolium, toltrazuril, diclazuril) are used in shuttle or rotation programmes to prevent resistance. Histomonostats (nitarsone, and historically dimetridazole) control blackhead disease in turkeys and occasionally layers; many have been withdrawn in the EU and are under review elsewhere. Always check the withdrawal period â typically 3â7 days for ionophores, longer for some chemicals â and never use a coccidiostat in layer feed intended for eggs sold to consumers without confirming local maximum residue limits.

Data Tables

Table 1. Typical inclusion rates and expected effects of key additives in African broiler and layer diets
Additive Typical inclusion Primary effect Commercial payback
Phytase500â1,000 FTU/kgReleases phytate P; saves DCP2â4% feed cost saving
Xylanase1,000â2,000 U/kg+2â4% digestible energyBetter FCR, drier litter
Protease10,000â20,000 U/kg+2â3% protein digestibilityLower soybean meal use
Probiotic (Bacillus/yeast)0.5â1 kg/tonneGut health, less mortality2â5% FCR gain in challenge
Organic acid blend0.5â2 kg/tonneLower gut pH, pathogen controlReduced medication cost
Essential oil blend100â300 g/tonneAntimicrobial, antioxidantAntibiotic-free premium
Antioxidant100â200 g/tonneProtects fats and vitaminsPreserves feed value
Mould inhibitor0.5â2 kg/tonnePrevents mould and mycotoxinAvoids flock loss
Ionophore coccidiostat60â125 g/tonnePrevents coccidiosisAvoids 5â15% mortality

Sources: FAO (2013), Good practices for the feed industry; NRC (1994), Nutrient Requirements of Poultry; industry product technical bulletins (BASF, DSM, Novus, Alltech) as cited in African feed mill practice.

Table 2. Withdrawal periods and regulatory considerations for selected additives in African markets
Additive class Typical withdrawal Key regulatory note
Ionophore coccidiostats3â7 daysNot permitted in layer feed for table eggs in many jurisdictions
Chemical coccidiostats5â10 daysCheck maximum residue limits (MRLs) in destination market
Histomonostats5â14 daysSeveral withdrawn; confirm national registration
Antibiotic growth promotersVariableBanned or restricted in EU, increasingly in African markets
Organic acidsNoneGenerally recognised as safe (GRAS)
EnzymesNoneRegister as feed additive; declare activity units
AntioxidantsNone at approved levelsMaximum limits apply (e.g., ethoxyquin)
Mycotoxin bindersNoneNot a substitute for rejecting contaminated grain

Sources: FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius (2013), Code of Practice on Good Animal Feeding; EU Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003 on feed additives; national registration requirements of Nigeria (NAFDAC), Kenya (KEBS), Ghana (FDA), and Zambia (ZAMRA).

â  SAFETY WARNING â READ BEFORE MIXING

Never exceed the manufacturer's recommended inclusion rate. Overdosing coccidiostats causes toxicity, reduced feed intake, and residues in meat and eggs. Ethoxyquin and some antioxidants have legal maximum limits. Mycotoxin binders do not make contaminated maize safe â reject grain above 20 ppb aflatoxin B1 for poultry feed, and never use mouldy grain for layer feed. Always observe withdrawal periods before slaughter or egg collection. Store additives in a cool, dry, locked store away from children and livestock, and keep a batch register with supplier, date, and quantity for traceability and regulatory inspection.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm the additive is registered for use in your country and for the target species (broiler vs. layer).
  2. Check the label for active ingredient, activity unit, inclusion rate, and expiry date.
  3. Verify the withdrawal period and record it on the feed formulation sheet.
  4. Weigh additives accurately â use a calibrated scale, not a scoop, for micro-ingredients.
  5. Pre-blend small quantities with a carrier before adding to the main mixer to avoid hot spots.
  6. Store in a cool, dry, dark place; keep opened bags sealed and use within the manufacturer's stated period.
  7. Keep a batch register: supplier, lot number, date received, date used, quantity.
  8. Review additive cost per tonne of feed against performance data every quarter and drop any product that does not pay for itself.

Further Reading

  • FAO (2013). Good practices for the feed industry â Implementing the Codex Alimentarius Code of Practice on Good Animal Feeding.
  • FAO. Protein sources for the animal feed industry.
  • EFSA. Feed additives â scientific opinions and authorisation status.
  • WHO/FAO. Codex Alimentarius â Code of Practice on Good Animal Feeding (CAC/RCP 54-2004).
  • African Union. Documents on animal feed and livestock development in Africa.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of adding phytase to poultry feed?
quiz.explanation: Phytase breaks down phytic acid, releasing phosphorus that chickens can absorb.

quiz.q: Which enzyme is most useful when feed contains more than 20% wheat?
quiz.explanation: Xylanase breaks down arabinoxylans in wheat, reducing gut viscosity.

quiz.q: What is a typical dose of phytase in poultry feed?
quiz.explanation: 500 FTU/kg is the standard recommended dose for most poultry diets.

quiz.q: How does protease help reduce feed cost?
options: B) It allows reduction of crude protein by 1%
quiz.explanation: Protease improves protein digestion, so you can lower crude protein without hurting performance.

quiz.q: Which of these is a prebiotic?
quiz.explanation: Mannan-oligosaccharides are non-digestible fibres that feed beneficial bacteria.

quiz.q: What is a synbiotic?
options: C) A combination of probiotic and prebiotic
quiz.explanation: Synbiotics combine a probiotic with a prebiotic for better gut health.

quiz.q: Why should you not mix probiotics with antibiotics?
options: B) Antibiotics kill the probiotic bacteria
quiz.explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria, including the beneficial probiotic strains.

quiz.q: What is a typical dose of probiotic in broiler feed?
quiz.explanation: 0.5-1 kg per tonne is the standard inclusion rate for most probiotic products.

quiz.q: Which organic acid is especially good for gut health?
quiz.explanation: Butyric acid feeds the cells lining the intestine, improving gut health.

quiz.q: What is a common active compound in oregano essential oil?
quiz.explanation: Oregano contains thymol and carvacrol; cinnamon contains cinnamaldehyde.

quiz.q: Why should organic acids be added after pelleting?
options: A) They are corrosive to the pellet mill
quiz.explanation: High temperatures during pelleting can degrade organic acids.

quiz.q: What is the main function of antioxidants in feed?
quiz.explanation: Antioxidants prevent oxidation of fats and oils, which causes rancidity.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural antioxidant?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin E (tocopherol) is a natural antioxidant, while the others are synthetic.

quiz.q: What moisture level in feed promotes mold growth?
quiz.explanation: Molds grow when feed moisture exceeds 12%.

quiz.q: Which mold inhibitor is commonly used at 0.1-0.3%?
quiz.explanation: Propionic acid is a common mold inhibitor in poultry feed.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for monensin in broilers?
quiz.explanation: Monensin has a 3-day withdrawal period before slaughter.

quiz.q: Which coccidiostat is an ionophore?
quiz.explanation: Monensin is an ionophore coccidiostat; the others are non-ionophores.

quiz.q: Why should layers not receive monensin after 16 weeks of age?
options: B) It causes residues in eggs
C) It is toxic to layers
quiz.explanation: Monensin can leave residues in eggs, so it is not allowed for laying hens.

quiz.q: What disease do histomonostats prevent?
quiz.explanation: Histomonostats are used to prevent histomoniasis, also known as blackhead disease.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural alternative to coccidiostats?
quiz.explanation: Garlic has some antibacterial and antiparasitic properties, though less effective than commercial drugs.

quiz.q: In Nigeria, which agency regulates feed additives?
quiz.explanation: NAFDAC is the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control in Nigeria.

quiz.q: What is the maximum EU limit for zinc oxide in feed?
quiz.explanation: The EU limits zinc oxide to 150 ppm in feed to reduce environmental pollution.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important for feed additives?
options: B) To track withdrawal periods and batch numbers
quiz.explanation: Records help ensure safe use, traceability, and compliance with regulations.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see bloody droppings in your flock?
quiz.explanation: Bloody droppings may indicate coccidiosis; a vet can diagnose and prescribe treatment.

quiz.q: Which additive is used to bind mycotoxins?
quiz.explanation: Bentonite is a clay that binds aflatoxins and other mycotoxins in the gut.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dose of essential oils in feed?
quiz.explanation: 100-300 mg/kg is the typical inclusion rate for essential oil blends.

quiz.q: Why should you store probiotics in a cool, dry place?
options: A) To prevent them from freezing
B) Heat kills the live bacteria
quiz.explanation: Probiotics contain live bacteria that are killed by high temperatures.

quiz.q: What is a shuttle program in coccidiosis control?
options: B) Rotating coccidiostats during the growing period
quiz.explanation: A shuttle program involves switching coccidiostats to prevent resistance.

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-ionophore coccidiostat?
quiz.explanation: Amprolium is a non-ionophore coccidiostat; the others are ionophores.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for amprolium in broilers?
quiz.explanation: Amprolium has a 3-day withdrawal period before slaughter.
